If the potentiality of modern communications failed those dedicated to waging war, how much more did it fail those professionally dedicated to preserving the peace. The tragedy of the diplomatic crisis that preceded the outbreak of the fighting in August 1914, which was to swell into the four-year tragedy of the Great War, is that events successively and progressively overwhelmed the capacity of statesmen and diplomats to control and contain them. Honourable and able men though they were, the servants of the chancelleries and foreign officers of the great powers in the July crisis were bound to the wheel of the written note, the encipherment routine, the telegraph schedule. The potentialities of the telephone, which might have cut across the barriers of communication, seem to have eluded their imaginative powers. The potentialities of the radio, available but unused, evaded them altogether.

In the event, the states of Europe proceeded, as if in a dead march and a dialogue to the deaf, to the destruction of their continent and its civilisation.

I've been thinking about the merits of Socialism and Autocracy, but don't have enough "mental playgrounds" to run with. Boiled down to a single topic, which do you guys think is better: a raising of the minimum standards (seen here) or the focused support of a few exceptional people (Mr. House in Fallout: New Vegas and Andrew Ryan of Bioshock come to mind).

At first glance, I would argue that steady improvement of an entire population would be best in the long run (literacy and hygiene have done wonders), but the implementation of this seems to boil things down to the lowest common denominator. It seems to dumb us down: holding back the exceptional and only allowing humanity to progress as fast as our slowest members.

On the other hand, nurturing exceptional people would put us on the "fast track" and gives the rest of us an example to aspire to. I would argue that giving the common man that inspiration, and then giving them a choice, would do more for humanity in the long run than mass general education would. Downsides are obviously rampant inequality and the possibility of moving "too fast" for society to keep up, creating a series of disasters that would otherwise be easily avoidable.
